How many times have you come up with a&nbsp; magnificent plan, showed it off to all your&nbsp;&nbsp; friends and family, been sure it is the solution&nbsp; to all your problems, only to have it die a slow&nbsp;&nbsp; death over the next few weeks? Many times we've&nbsp; all done it, so I'm not pointing fingers here.&nbsp;&nbsp; That's because coming up with a strategy is&nbsp; much easier than executing it, and this is&nbsp;&nbsp; where this book comes into play. The authors&nbsp; came up with four disciplines of execution.&nbsp;&nbsp; It's a system that makes achieving goals totally&nbsp; possible.

The four principles are focus, leverage,&nbsp;&nbsp; engagement, and accountability. If all this&nbsp; sounds super general, it is because it is. But,&nbsp;&nbsp; before we show it off and move one to the next&nbsp; video, let me tell you the secret sauce. It is&nbsp;&nbsp; how you apply this principle that matters,&nbsp; and the four DX framework does it in a very&nbsp;&nbsp; particular way, so let's get cracking. Number one is focus, but what does that even&nbsp;&nbsp; mean? Stay with me. In this very first step. We&nbsp; choose three goals to focus on. The author calls&nbsp;&nbsp; this wildly important goals or WIGs.

These are&nbsp; medium to long term goals that drive your life.&nbsp;&nbsp; Things like have $1.2 million invested in the&nbsp; stock market by the age of 40, or lose 5 kgs by&nbsp;&nbsp; June 2022, or get promoted to senior manager by&nbsp; the age of 30. These are basically any goals that&nbsp;&nbsp; you would consider wildly important for your life.&nbsp; There is no right, there is no wrong here. Only&nbsp;&nbsp; you know what drives you. These goals need to be&nbsp; challenging, but attainable. That's all fine and&nbsp;&nbsp; dandy, but how do you even come up with these&nbsp; goals in the first place?

There are four steps&nbsp;&nbsp; to settling on a wildly important goal. First, it all starts by brainstorming. Ask&nbsp;&nbsp; yourself what kind of change would have the&nbsp; most impact on your life. Think of things that&nbsp;&nbsp; are not currently working, or the things that&nbsp; if they're made to work a little bit better,&nbsp;&nbsp; would have a dramatic impact on your life. Now,&nbsp; list them all out. Next, you need to assess.&nbsp;&nbsp; Out of everything you listed, which three&nbsp; would have the overall highest impact? Now&nbsp;&nbsp; you need to test your potential goals, and&nbsp; there are two main considerations here.&nbsp;&nbsp; Is it measurable?

Is there a way to keep score of&nbsp; your progress? If the answer is no, it is not a&nbsp;&nbsp; good candidate because the scoring system would&nbsp; help keep you motivated. Second, does it depend&nbsp;&nbsp; mainly on you? If you need to enlist outside&nbsp; help for more than 20% of your goal, it might&nbsp;&nbsp; be a challenge. When things depend on outside&nbsp; factors or other people, the challenge for you&nbsp;&nbsp; is even greater. Finally, state, or put simply,&nbsp; write it all down. Be specific and concise. &nbsp; Now let's look at an example. This is Mike. He's&nbsp; really excited to start executing his plans,&nbsp;&nbsp; and aren't we all?

Mike takes out a piece of paper&nbsp; and lists all the goals that are important to him.&nbsp;&nbsp; These are things like become more healthy, save&nbsp; more money, get a dog, buy a dependable car,&nbsp;&nbsp; travel the world, and so on. When he assesses&nbsp; things and test them as we talked about,&nbsp;&nbsp; he realizes that becoming more healthy or buying&nbsp; a dependable car will have the most impact on his&nbsp;&nbsp; life. But, they're not very measurable,&nbsp; at least not yet. Let's transform them.&nbsp;&nbsp; Become more healthy becomes to lose 5 kgs by March&nbsp; 2022. Buy a dependable car becomes buy a Toyota&nbsp;&nbsp; RAV4, two to three years old at a cost of no more&nbsp; than 30K by April 2022.

Now we're talking. These&nbsp;&nbsp; are specific goals that depend solely on Mike, and&nbsp; have a specific deadline and way to keep track of.&nbsp;&nbsp; WIGs done. Good job, Mike. Now comes leverage. In this discipline,&nbsp;&nbsp; you learn how to get from point A to point&nbsp; B. Imagine that your point A is a huge heavy&nbsp;&nbsp; rock. No matter how hard you push against it,&nbsp; it's not going to move. But, if you apply a little&nbsp;&nbsp; lever, the rock starts to move, and not by a&nbsp; lot, but it does move and in the right direction.&nbsp;&nbsp; The second discipline is all about finding the&nbsp; right lever so you can move your goals from&nbsp;&nbsp; point A to point B.

Points A and B are what the&nbsp; author calls lag measures. These are results. They&nbsp;&nbsp; are very important, as they tell you if you've&nbsp; reached your goals or not. Have you lost weight,&nbsp;&nbsp; have you enough money, and so on. The&nbsp; lever in the rock is called a lead measure,&nbsp;&nbsp; and lead measures quantify the actions&nbsp; that have the most impact on your goals. &nbsp; Now back to Mike for an example. His lag measures&nbsp; are, right now, he's 70 kgs, which is point A,&nbsp;&nbsp; and he wants to be 65, point B. His lead measures&nbsp; are the how he'll get to achieve those goals.&nbsp;&nbsp; How does one lose weight?

Less calories in&nbsp; and more exercise and physical activity.&nbsp;&nbsp; This is a good time to mention that a good lead&nbsp; measure has two characteristics. First of all,&nbsp;&nbsp; it's predictive. A change in the lead measure&nbsp; must create a change in the lag measure. Two,&nbsp;&nbsp; it's influenceable. You must be able to influence&nbsp; it without dependence on someone else. If Mike is&nbsp;&nbsp; to restrict his calories, it will for sure lead&nbsp; to a faster weight loss, so it's predictive.&nbsp;&nbsp; Who controls how much and what Mike eats? Mike,&nbsp; so his calorie intake is also influenceable.&nbsp;&nbsp; If Mike concentrates on actions that most&nbsp; influence his goals, his goals become not an if,&nbsp;&nbsp; but a when.

The less he eats and the more he&nbsp; exercises, the faster he'll get to point B. &nbsp; Now, let's move on. Number three is engagement.&nbsp; How do you best engage into a goal? By keeping&nbsp;&nbsp; a compelling scorecard. Humans are naturally wired&nbsp; to compete. We become highly motivated and engaged&nbsp;&nbsp; where there is an opportunity to win. Just look at&nbsp; every sport on the planet. The goal is always to&nbsp;&nbsp; win, to have a better score. The moment you take&nbsp; the score away, people stop trying so hard. Let's&nbsp;&nbsp; use this hard wired tendency to your advantage.

If&nbsp; you're like Mike, right now you might be thinking,&nbsp;&nbsp; "That's all nice, but I want to lose weight,&nbsp; and there's no one to compete with." True,&nbsp;&nbsp; so how about you compete with yourself? Come up&nbsp; with your own scorecard that forces you to act. &nbsp; A good scorecard has three requirements.&nbsp; First of all, it is simple. A more minimal&nbsp;&nbsp; scorecard is much easier to update. Think of any&nbsp; competitive sport. It usually has a simple score,&nbsp;&nbsp; and time left in the game. It is a scorecard, not&nbsp; a spreadsheet, so keep it simple. A good scorecard&nbsp;&nbsp; is also visible.

Put it next to your bed, on your&nbsp; bathroom mirror. Whatever it is in your case,&nbsp;&nbsp; you should not have to turn on your laptop or&nbsp; log into a site to update it. Finally, a good&nbsp;&nbsp; scorecard is quickly readable. Anyone looking&nbsp; at it should be able to tell within seconds&nbsp;&nbsp; if you're winning or losing. In the case of Mike,&nbsp; he makes a simple scorecard that keeps track of&nbsp;&nbsp; his daily calories and time spent exercising, and&nbsp; sticks it on his fridge. Three disciplines down,&nbsp;&nbsp; one more to go. Give it up for Mike. Finally, the last one is accountability.&nbsp;&nbsp; Disciplines one to three are to set up the&nbsp; execution.

In discipline four is where the&nbsp;&nbsp; action is. Without the accountability piece,&nbsp; the goal will eventually be overtaken by what&nbsp;&nbsp; the author calls the whirlwind, or just the&nbsp; day to day menial, trivial tasks. Basically,&nbsp;&nbsp; accountability is what will ensure you are&nbsp; staying on course. There are two parts to the&nbsp;&nbsp; accountability discipline that you need&nbsp; in order to make this step productive.&nbsp;&nbsp; Accountability needs to be precise and regularly&nbsp; scheduled. Here's how it works for Mike. He&nbsp;&nbsp; schedules 15 minutes every Sunday evening for an&nbsp; accountability session.

The idea is to quickly&nbsp;&nbsp; review his last seven days progress, and see&nbsp; things like what went well, what didn't go well,&nbsp;&nbsp; how can he do better next week. He narrows down&nbsp; the specific issues he face, and comes up with&nbsp;&nbsp; a precise solution to over the pitfalls. The continuous review and adjustment will&nbsp;&nbsp; make sure not only that he stays on course, but&nbsp; that he's continually improving. Not to mention,&nbsp;&nbsp; the personal satisfaction of seeing his progress&nbsp; week after week will keep him happy and motivated.&nbsp;&nbsp; If you followed along this far, you saw how&nbsp; Mike went from being caught in the whirlwind of&nbsp;&nbsp; day to day tasks, to figure out what his wildly&nbsp; important goals are, and then he took the most&nbsp;&nbsp; important step: the execution of the plan.

After&nbsp; all, the book is called The Four Disciplines Of&nbsp;&nbsp; Execution, not the four steps of&nbsp; making a plan, feeling good about it,&nbsp;&nbsp; and never implement it. Right now, you're either&nbsp; super motivated to get started, or you're little&nbsp;&nbsp; bit confused because this is a rather complex&nbsp; system.
